To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the expression of Escherichia Coli adhesins is controlled by phase-variable genetic switch, which can lead to a sequential expression of the adhesins during the infection.

(i) E. coli phase-variable genes are expressed in a sequential manner; (ii) the expression of one phase-variable locus influences the expression of other phase-variable loci; (iii) the sequential expression of the loci leads to a programmed expression pattern that is beneficial during infection; (iv) the programmed pattern of expression is a form of bacterial memory; and (v) the programmed pattern is maintained by a feedback loop that involves a phase-variable locus and a quorum-sensing system

(i) the expression of virulence genes is controlled by a complex network of regulatory elements that are often phase-variable and (ii) this network can lead to a co-ordinated or sequential expression of virulence loci that is analogous to electronic memory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of adherence in Escherichiacoli, and in particular, the role of the phase-variable O antigen and fimbriae.
the mechanisms that underpin the expression of virulence factors in Escherichicoli and the consequences of this for bacterial behaviour.
the mechanisms that control the expression of virulence genes in bacteria
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the bacterial surface structures that mediate adherence and motility in E. coli have evolved a complex and sophisticated regulatory network that is capable of producing a range of phenotypic responses to environmental signals.

the expression of adherence factors is controlled by a complex network of switches, cross-talk and a form of memory that is likely to be of considerable significance to pathogenesis and the development of vaccines.
the expression of virulence factors is a highly complex process that is likely to involve a combination of random, stochastic, and co-ordinated control.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression of the type 1 fimbriae, curli and flagella in Escherichiacoli is controlled by a complex network of interactions.
the expression of the major fimbrial adhesin F1C in the presence of the flagellar antigen FliC leads to a switch from a motile, nonadherent phenotype to a nonmotile, adherent phenotype.
the expression of virulence genes is not simply a random event, but is subject to control and co-ordination.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic switches that regulate expression of the fimbrial adhesins are not random but rather are under complex control that is dependent on the growth environment and other virulence genes.
there are many examples of co-regulation of virulence factors in pathogenic bacteria.
there is a strong link between the expression of different adherence factors and that this is likely to be of benefit to the bacteria.
